When is wealth liquid?

When Is Wealth Liquid?Gold and Household
Financial Constraints in India

Vivek Gupta · Fiorella Pizzolon · Aditi Singh

Read latest paper →
A household can own assets and still struggle to sustain spending when income falls. This talk asks how the form of wealth changes the way we identify financially constrained households.

Wealth is not cash in hand

Owning an asset does not automatically make it available for current spending.

Owning wealth does not make it ready to spend. A home provides shelter and gold stores value. Paying today’s bills requires cash, or a way to turn an asset into cash.

Why focus on gold rather than land/house?

Gold can provide cash more quickly and with less paperwork than a home. Selling or borrowing against housing involves finding a buyer or lender, checking ownership documents and valuing the property. Both assets can be collateral, but they differ in how readily households can use them.

India has an established market for loans against gold. The World Gold Council describes this as a route to short-term finance. The Household Finance Committee documents gold’s broad acceptance as collateral and barriers to borrowing against real estate.

Use Own, Sell and Pledge to compare ownership, a sale and a gold-backed loan. A loan adds cash and liabilities, not net wealth. Both land and housing can serve as collateral, but gold can be turned into cash more readily.

Testing the predictions

Held-out households show how well the models recover income and wealth.

Income prediction uses a 20% CPHS testing holdout of 25,759 households. Gradient boosting has total-income R² 0.8170. Explore each method’s actual testing metrics. Distribution images retain their source axes and legends.

Why half a month’s income?

A household living from paycheck to paycheck can still have cash on the day it is interviewed. If a ₹10,000 paycheck arrives at the start of the month and is spent steadily, cash falls to zero before the next payment. Its average balance is ₹5,000.

Following Kaplan, Violante and Weidner (2014), that average gives us a benchmark for identifying limited liquidity. Survey balances are a snapshot within the payment cycle.

The rule uses net liquid wealth: liquid assets minus liquid liabilities. For nonnegative balances, a household is HtM when this is no more than half its monthly income. For borrowers, the rule measures remaining borrowing room, assuming an unsecured limit of one month’s income.

HtM = hand-to-mouth. “Poor” and “wealthy” identify balance-sheet groups, not income ranks. Framework: Kaplan, Violante and Weidner (2014).

Introduce the liquidity test before the poor–wealthy distinction. Within HtM households, net illiquid wealth distinguishes poor from wealthy HtM. The group names are not statements about a household’s rank in the income distribution. Gold can enter the balance sheet in several different ways.

Who has gold-collateral capacity?

Separate wealthy HtM households by whether gold can bridge their liquid shortfall.

Gold is illiquid, 75% pledgeable, with no minimum holding. CPHS: Poor HtM 1.48%; Wealthy HtM, with capacity 29.20%; Wealthy HtM, without capacity 18.63%; Non-HtM 50.70%. Survey-weighted classification population: 128,794 households. These groups do not add the housing-quality adjustment.

Gold changes the classification

Counting gold as liquid expands the group with a usable spending buffer.

In CPHS, non-HtM is 50.70% with gold excluded and 83.12% with gold liquid. Gold illiquid changes the poor–wealthy split without changing the liquid-buffer test. This is a classification comparison, not a policy experiment.

How much gold is pledgeable?

The capacity test depends on the share of gold value available to borrow against.

The preferred fraction is 75%, with no minimum holding. Select another fraction or minimum holding to examine sensitivity. Capacity requires net liquid wealth plus pledgeable eligible gold to exceed half of monthly income. Every displayed share comes from a aggregate, not a new calculation on household records.

Housing value and housing quality

Housing adjustments change the poor–wealthy split within hand-to-mouth households.

The real-estate screen excludes specified unusable items and low-value holdings, with ₹100,000 as the preferred value threshold. Low infrastructure means at least two of three markers: mud or unburnt-brick walls, a non-concrete roof, and no water source inside the house. The infrastructure comparison has its own interview sample; do not combine its percentages with the separate housing-value or gold-capacity samples.

The preferred combined definition

The proposed grouping combines housing quality with collateralizable gold.

Gold illiquid + ₹100,000 housing screen + Two of three infrastructure markers + 75% gold capacity

Introduce shock persistence before showing estimates. An elasticity of .20 means a 1% income change corresponds to a .20% consumption change. An MPC of .20 means 20 paise per rupee. These illustrative values explain units, not additional estimates.

Annual consumption responses

Compare responses across household balance sheets.

Default: annual BPP MA(2), two-year consumption response, full sample, survey weighted, direct MPC units. G1: MPC 0.133714, SE 0.005119, 22,692 households; G2: MPC 0.113257, SE 0.004308, 29,557 households; G3: MPC 0.099094, SE 0.002896, 70,774 households. G1 combines poor, low-infrastructure wealthy, and high-infrastructure wealthy without gold capacity; G2 is high-infrastructure wealthy with capacity; G3 is non-HtM. The separate housing-value screen is not applied.

Three annual estimation approaches

Each approach uses a different feature of the income and consumption panel.

BPP

Fit income and consumption second moments to separate permanent and transitory innovations.

Commault

Use future income growth to identify the response to a temporary income change.

Crawley–Kuchler

Compare consumption and income changes across change lengths.

Use the previous slide’s controls to compare annual specifications. Group rankings depend on the method and specification.

BPP is Blundell, Pistaferri and Preston (2008). Commault’s lead-three specification is the initial alternative. Crawley–Kuchler uses the change-length combinations. The baseline trimming rule is common across methods, while each estimator and sample window retains its own construction. This deck contains annual MPC records only.

Months are relative to the later interview. Outcomes are four-month sums in constant-2014 rupees. Prior wage workers are aged 25–62.

Month 0 is the unemployment interview. Both horizons compare with baseline months −8 to −5. Transition covers −4 to −1; recovery covers 0 to 3. Each requires its own financial months and retains zeros. Controls remain employed and have no other qualifying household job loss. Outcomes are four-month sums, not monthly means.

Spending and wages after job loss

Relate the change in household spending to the change in the worker’s wages.

Revised transition total-consumption IV: 0.11611544, SE 0.00866098, 95% interval [0.09914007, 0.13309080]. Sample: 733,280 observation pairs, 130,106 households, 3,891 job-loss pairs. Compare recovery, food consumption, first stage and reduced form using the controls. This is separate from the annual income-shock MPC exercise.

Wealth composition and financial constraints

01Gold changes who is classified as constrained. Liquid-gold and collateral-capacity definitions reveal different ways to access wealth.

02Consumption responses depend on the exercise. Annual income innovations and observed job loss provide distinct comparisons.

03Complementary surveys connect balance sheets to household spending. Predictions, classifications and response estimates retain their own samples.

Gold treatment changes measured financial constraints. Current annual responses combine housing quality with gold capacity. The separate housing-value screen is not added. Job-loss estimates use their own four-group classification and employed-worker comparison. Keep these samples and definitions distinct.

Income prediction distributions

This is the original testing-sample figure. Black is observed, blue is preferred gradient boosting, with additional methods identified by the figure legend. Its positive-income sample and natural-log rupee axis are preserved. No histogram bins were reconstructed from the image.

Positive wealth distributions

The controls switch between the original baseline aggregates and component figures. These images retain their plotted ranges, units and source legends. Zero shares refer to all testing households under the original figure definitions. Images are responsive; no synthetic interactive bins are added.

Samples and units

Annual estimation sample

2019-classified households with someone aged 25–64. Positive income and consumption; CPI-deflated values; calendar-month 1st–99th percentile trimming of ratios to mean real monthly income. Annual observations require at least eight months. Main estimates use survey weights and normalized income and consumption levels, with household-level uncertainty. Unweighted and first-stage-control alternatives are available.

Job-loss estimation sample

Prior wage workers aged 25–62; complete financial coverage for the selected transition or recovery windows; zeros retained. Unweighted IV controls for age, age squared, sex, prior wages and state-by-endpoint-month effects. Uncertainty clusters by household. Group comparisons start in 2022 and use fixed 2019 classifications.

Classification populations and uncertainty

Shares are survey-weighted percentages of classification populations. Annual chart lines show one standard error; job-loss charts use 95% confidence intervals. A different sample, definition or unit is always labeled separately.

The full sample window includes the COVID period with interactions; pre-COVID is 2014–2019, post-COVID 2021–2025. Total consumption excludes self-production in the annual exercise. The job-loss exercise has its own consumption and timing definitions. The deck has no household records and performs no new estimation.
